title: Latin Grammys Full Winners List: Rosalía Wins Big With Album and Song of the Year Honors
description: The 2026 Latin Grammys took place on Nov. 12 at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas. Going into the evening, Edgar Barrera led the nominees wit
body:
The 2026 Latin Grammys took place on Nov. 12 at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas. Going into the evening, Edgar Barrera led the nominees with ten nods, followed by Jorge Drexler, Rosalía, Karol G and Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso with seven each. See the full winners list below.

	Album of the Year: “Lux (Complete Works)” – Rosalía

	Song of the Year: “La Perla” – Noah Goldstein, David Rodríguez, Rosalía, Ryan Tedder & Dylan Wiggins, songwriters (Rosalía featuring Yahritza y Su Esencia)
	

	Record of the Year: “Niño” – Milo J

	Best Alternative Album: “Lux” – Rosalía 

	Best Pop Song: “La Perla” – Rosalía (featuring Yahritza y Su Esencia) 

	Best Short Form Music Video: “Sauvignon Blanc” – Rosalía 

	Best Urban Music Album: “Tropicoqueta” – Karol G 

	Best Pop/Rock Album: “JuanEsteban” – Juanes 

	Best Electronic Music Performance: “Beto’s Horns – Fred Remix” – CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso with Fred Again.. 

	Best Pop/Rock Song: “Hasta Jesús Tuvo Un Mal Día” – CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso with Sting 

	Best Long Form Music Video: “FREE SPIRITS (The Film)” – CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso 

	Best Folk Music Album: “La Vida Es Más Corta” – Milo J 

	Best Urban/Urban Fusion Performance: “Gil” – Milo J featuring Trueno 

	Best Recording Package: Milo J 

	Best Latin Jazz/Jazz Album: “Gonzalo Plays Pino” – Gonzalo Rubalcaba 

	Best Rap/Hip Hop Song: “Antisistema” – J Noa & Trooko 

	Best Christian Album (Spanish Language): “Inquebrantable” – Marcos Witt, Marco Barrientos & Marcos Vidal 
	

	Best New Artist: Aria Vega 

	Best Contemporary Mexican Album: “Dosis” – Xavi 

	Best Contemporary Tropical Album: “Antes Que El Tiempo Se Vaya” – Fonseca 

	Best Tejano Album: “Bobby Pulido & Friends: Una Tuya y Una Mía (Vol. 2/En Vivo)” – Bobby Pulido 

	Best Roots Song: “El tambor chico” – Facundo Balta & Jorge Drexler (songwriters: Facundo Balta & Jorge Drexler)

title: ‘The Body’ Creator on the Dance Team’s Sexuality, What Happened to Grace and Whether God Is Real
description:
Nov 12, 2026 7:00pm PT	
	

	
	‘The Body’ Creator on the Dance Team’s Sexuality, What Happened to Grace and Whether God Is Real
body:
Nov 12, 2026 7:00pm PT	
	

	
	‘The Body’ Creator on the Dance Team’s Sexuality, What Happened to Grace and Whether God Is Real
	



			
			
	
						

									Courtesy of Netflix
	
					


							
		

	SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for “The Body,” now streaming on Netflix.

	If you’re looking for clear answers about whether or not God is real in the world of “The Body” — Netflix’s spooky new drama series about mass hysteria originating from a Catholic school dance team — you’re not going to find them.

	“If we ever fully defined it, it would break the rule of the show,” says creator Quinn Shephard. “The show is meant to mimic faith, so there’s people who believe, there’s people who don’t and there’s people in the middle, like me, who are like, ‘I don’t know.’”

	But regardless of whether it’s the big man upstairs or just some devious teenage girls pulling the strings, “The Body” has a lot to say about faith and its role in the lives of young and sometimes queer girls. Shephard is a proud lesbian who was raised in the church and has stepped away from it without fully rejecting it, and the show’s up-and-down relationship with God is a product of that.

	At the beginning of “The Body,” a devout Catholic named Grace (Sofia Wylie) is the clear standout at dance team tryouts, much to the chagrin of some of the team’s more senior members, who roll their eyes at her rule-following innocence. Thus, she’s put through a bit of hazing: At a Halloween party at an abandoned convent, she’s pressured to take Ecstasy by Elise (Sara Boustany), the team’s co-captain and resident badass, as everyone jokingly perform a ritual meant to sacrifice her soul to the devil. But the devil doesn’t seem to know that they’re joking. Anya (Kristina Bogic), who is Elise’s co-captain and the most popular girl in school, notices that Grace has wandered off alone. Alongside Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), an awkward new girl who got rejected from the team in favor of Grace, she finds Grace on the ground, convulsing until she passes out. Anya and Lisbeth decide to take her to a hospital, but on the way, Grace appears to die. Because Anya supplied the Ecstasy, she’s terrified she’ll get in trouble. Lisbeth sees this as her way onto the dance team and into Anya’s good graces, and takes charge. They take Grace’s body back to her own house and tuck her into bed, then use Grace’s phone to text a friend that she got home safe, giving themselves plausible deniability. But at the end of the first episode, Grace takes a breath.


	She doesn’t wake all the way up, though, and spends the rest of the season in a coma as the dance team is wracked with guilt about the Ecstasy, which they don’t confess about. Needing support from the only other person who knows what happened, Anya brings Lisbeth onto the dance team to take Grace’s place, which intensifies the conflict between Anya and Elise. The two best friends are clearly in love with each other, and had been fooling around sexually at the party, but Anya insists that she’s straight and loyal to her boyfriend, Steven (Orlando Norman). Frustrated by Anya’s new closeness to Lisbeth, and with latent suspicion about Anya’s role in what happened to Grace, Elise fakes a spiritual experience, shrieking in front of the whole school that she’s having a vision of Grace. But everyone on the team — except Anya and Lisbeth, of course — buys into it. One by one, they begin faking their own visions. Soon, the whole town starts to believe that Grace is all-powerful, chosen by God to perform healing miracles from her apparent deathbed. People gather on her family’s lawn to worship her.



	

					Left to right: Kyra Pierce as Bailey, Sarah Abbot as Olivia, Michela Luci as Amy, Kristina Bogic as Anya, Shirley Chen as Maddie
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	Lisbeth is delighted, using her relationship with Anya to increase her social standing at school and to protect her brother, Leo (Jackson Kelly), who at one point drew suspicion because of his crush on (and lewd drawings of) Grace. But eventually, Elise pieces together the truth, forcing Anya to confess to Father Franklin (Nnamdi Asomugha), the school principal and pastor. At that exact moment, though, Grace finally wakes up. Weakly, she whispers, “I’m God.”

	Shepherd spoke with Variety about Catholicism, lesbian camp and who-slash-what God is.


	
		Anya and Elise’s relationship feels lived-in and very unique — there’s not a lot of media set in the early aughts that depicts queer teens. How did you approach their hot-and-cold friendship and romance? Were you pulling from anything in particular?	

	I definitely put so much of myself into those two characters, and also some of my close friends who let me use their stories. I do find the era really interesting, because it wasn’t like being gay was illegal, or like you’re guaranteed to get disowned, but it was definitely not good. And it felt like the biggest threat was to your femininity, and your social standing as normal or cool. I didn’t go to high school in 2004; I was in high school a little later than that. But pre-smartphones and pre-gay marriage being legalized, that was a very specific era. Being lesbian felt like a bit. I remember my friends and I doing so many bits where we’d “pretend” to be gay for each other. It’s not that it wasn’t being talked about; it’s that it wasn’t cool. I was like, “I can’t be gay.” This is going to sound so bad, but I think I thought I had to be butch. I didn’t want to, like, get a short haircut and start wearing rainbow knee socks.

	For Anya, that’s her worst fear. She’s not ready. She’s quite high femme, and on the top of the social hierarchy, and she’s like, “Oh my God. Not only am I going to threaten that, but I have to give up on all these ideas of what my life is going to be? Are people going to act differently around me in the locker room? Am I going to lose my girlhood? Am I going to lose my status?” And we talked a lot in the room about how much Catholicism plays into Anya’s fears — it is a fear that she’s going to go to hell, but it’s not the main fear. Certainly, a piece of her shame comes from Catholicism, but I think it’s more interesting and more relatable to more people that she’s equally afraid, if not more afraid, that she’s just gonna lose her identity.

	Because of that, even though she also has a lot of kindness to her, she does a lot of really fucked up things. I wanted to make a very unsanitized, messy first queer love story. I was seeing too many shows where the characters are gay and it’s totally fine and no one has a problem with it. Like, there’s the parent who’s a little homophobic, and then there’s one conversation where they’re like, “Actually, I love you, honey.” No. It’s messy as hell. And you do some crazy stuff that you look back on, like, “Why did I do that?” I really wanted to give that to Anya and Elise.




	

					Sara Boustany as Elise, Kristina Bogic as Anya
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	
		Tell me about queerness as it exists — if it exists — elsewhere on the dance team. With Lisbeth, for example, it’s never totally clear whether she has any latent attraction to Anya.	

	I like to joke that with the amount of queer women involved in making the show, the core ethos and tone is so inherently like lesbian camp and a lesbian sense of humor. That even applies to the fact that there’s a lot of really lovable men in the story. The men are kind of innocent, and that’s from a lot of the women working on the show being like, “With the men that I dated, it wasn’t their fault that I wasn’t into them. It was me and my journey, and God, what I put that guy through!” Everyone in the show is linked to that twisted sense of humor and trying to turn shame and trauma into comedy. But we’ve got stuff to play with in Season 2 in terms of queer characters.

	I actually really like that people have debates about Lisbeth. Because to make her relationship with Anya about sexuality would almost be too simple. I think it’s way bigger than that. Lisbeth’s character isn’t driven by sexuality, almost at all. She’s more driven by survival. She’s a child of trauma, and she’s got some slightly asexual and sociopathic tendencies coming out, but I don’t think that’s necessarily who she is forever. It’s more that that’s where we meet her, because she’s in survival mode.


	
		Like Anya, she does things that feel a bit evil, but she’s also really charming, and it’s clear how her past drove her to make these decisions. She always keeps calm because she has to, but what’s her internal monologue saying as she’s trying to control this secret she and Anya have about Grace? Is she secretly freaking out?	

	I love Lisbeth. I don’t think she’s inherently bad. I just think she’s opportunistic in the first season, and too smart for her own good. It’s almost frustrating to her how ahead of other people her brain is. She’s definitely a bit on the spectrum. She struggles with social cues, but she’s brilliant, and she can’t help but see opportunities and strategies. For me, the lovable part of her is that she can strategize a takeover. She can play three-dimensional chess. She is starting mass hysteria to protect her brother and gain access to the dance team. 

	But at the end of the day, she doesn’t know how to act like a normal high-school girl at a party. She can’t do it. She tries so hard, and she literally studies it like gospel, but she can’t get there, and I think that’s so human. Sometimes it feels like there’s a way to study something and get there, but you can’t because that’s not how life works. And she had such a profound relationship with religion when she was younger that she lost. It’s like she’s searching for something that profound again, and when she finds it, she’s literally not going to be stopped. She’s a dog with a bone. If she wants to be on that dance team, she’s getting on that dance team no matter what, even if she has to hide a body. She’s getting there.




	

					Geena Meszaros as Lisbeth
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	
		Outside of the question of her sexuality, how does she feel about Anya? Is Anya just a pathway to popularity, or does she have any genuine love for her as a friend?	

	I think it’s both. It changes. There are scenes where she’s like, “I’m so enamored with this girl. I wish I could be just like her. I don’t know if I want to be with her, be like her, be around her or be inside her skin. I don’t know. I’m just obsessed.” And then there’s other times where she’s like, “This girl is on my nerves.” It’s very hard for Lisbeth when Anya is like, “Why are you not freaking out?” And she’s like, “I am, but this is how I freak out.” She doesn’t understand Anya, but there are moments, like when she sees that Anya’s working on her dance team jacket, and Anya’s letting her into her closet, that’s like the happiest day of Lisbeth’s life. She’s like, “I finally have a friend, and I’m so happy.” Does she have some ulterior motives? Yeah. But there’s also a really wholesome motive in there too. She wants a friend.


	
		What went into the writing of Maddie (Shirley Chen)? For much of the season, she’s the only one being truthful about the fact that she isn’t seeing visions of Grace. When she does become a Grace worshiper at the end, has she genuinely convinced herself she sees her? Or is she lying too?	

	Maddie’s quite an earnest character. I don’t feel like she’s ever purposefully deceiving. She really struggles with the lies that the girls are telling. One of the writers, Lily Houghton, told a story about how she lost both her parents. They were very beloved, and so many people came up to her, like, “Your dad came to me in a dream. I saw your mom yesterday, and she came with messages.” And she got to the point where she was like, “I don’t want to hear people’s stories about my parents visiting them, because if they’re going to visit someone, why would they not visit me?” And it was such a personal, vivid story. We were all so moved. It’s so human to still feel like a kid, like, “I feel like it would be me,” and also the bigger picture of people claiming someone else’s loss. So we baked a lot of that into Maddie’s desire to see Grace, and I would say she ends the show believing. And that gets validated, because she’s the one who says that when everyone confesses, that’s when Grace is going to wake up, and then that happens. She’s going to be telling anyone who will listen that she got a prophecy. I think she’s like,”My best friend is God, and it’s cool.”




	

					Shirley Chen as Maddie 
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	
		Can you answer whether the show believes in the supernatural? And does it believe in God?	

	The rule that we have internally is that the show’s perspective on the supernatural needs to mimic a relationship with faith. So you can choose how you want to view the events that are presented. For every supernatural theory, there needs to be a countertheory, and the audience needs to be empowered to decide which show they’re watching and which character they align with. When people are like, “What is happening for you?” I’m like, “I don’t know! I don’t know what happens after we die. I don’t know the meaning of life. I don’t know exactly what God is.” The people making the show still have questions, so the show still has questions, and that’s the rule.


	
		So there’s a spiritual perspective, and a supernatural perspective, and it’s both/and instead of either/or. But would you say that, in the world of the show, there is absolutely something happening beyond human understanding? Or is there also a version of the show where every event has been orchestrated by the characters and is grounded in scientific reality?	

	To me, that’s the same as being like, “On Earth, is there a God? Or is there not?” It is impossible for me to answer. And have a similar attitude with the show. The show exists in the unknown space. With the ending, there are clear supernatural and grounded, scientific theories that can explain that, and that’s the crux of the question we go into the next season with.

	It’s part of why I love and gravitate towards spiritual journalism — journalism that follows people’s unexplainable events. I like material without an agenda, that’s just like, “This has happened to this many people. We don’t know what it means.” People say that when you have a near-death experience, your brain fires your neurons and it gives you this crazy hallucination. And then there’s this camp of people who says you’re really seeing the afterlife. But, literally, we can’t know. Unless we die. So I don’t know! If we ever fully defined it, it would break the rule of the show. The show is meant to mimic faith, so there’s people who believe, there’s people who don’t and there’s people in the middle, like me, who are like, “I don’t know.”




	

					Sofia Wylie as Grace
									COURTESY OF NETFLIX
	



	
		Since you’re hopeful for a Season 2, what can you say about the ending and what you hope to cover in the future? Thematically, what’s going on in that moment where Grace wakes up and says that she’s God?	

	We always knew the ending going into the first season, and I think that moment is so fun because it provokes exactly the conversation that we’ve been having in the writers’ room. We hear Michael say that people can hear things in comas sometimes, so there’s a part of you that goes, “Maybe she’s been hearing everyone talking about these theories, and she knows.” We also have heard countless stories in life about people in comas, or people who have died and come back, who have these crazy visions. Did she experience the afterlife? Has she changed? Did something happen to her soul? Is it supernatural? And also, since she’s waking up from a coma, is she going to remember what she says? People say and do crazy things when they’re waking up from comas they have no memory of. The fact that people are excited to discuss their theory on what that ending means is exactly what I want. Without saying too much, it’s a perfect encapsulation of what we’d like to do with the next season.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: ‘The Body’ Creator on the Dance Team’s Sexuality, What Happened to Grace and Whether God Is Real

title: Savannah Guthrie Extends Contract With NBC News
description:
Savannah Guthrie‘s tenure at “Today” still has a lot of tomorrow in it.

	Guthrie has extended her current deal with NBC News, according to a perso
body:
Savannah Guthrie‘s tenure at “Today” still has a lot of tomorrow in it.

	Guthrie has extended her current deal with NBC News, according to a person familiar with the matter, a move that will keep her at the desk of the network’s flagship “Today” program at a time when the show has surged ahead of its main competitors in the ratings. The move will also serve to tamp down speculation about the journalist’s interest in remaining in her role after having suffered an immense family tragedy — the unsolved abduction of her mother, Nancy — in public.
	

	NBC News declined to make executives available for comment. The Breaker newsletter previously reported on Guthrie’s contract extension.

	The anchor’s deal was believed to expire later this year or in early 2027, and NBC News’ decision to continue its relationship with her runs counter to current TV-news trends. Indeed, top anchors such as Hoda Kotb, Neal Cavuto, Chris Wallace and others have exited places such as NBC News, Fox News and CNN as media companies scrutinize their expenses in the streaming era and while their corporate owners mull new arrangements that may leave them smaller or smushed into a larger conglomerate. Comcast, NBC’s owner, intends to spin off the company in a few months’ time, leaving it significantly smaller than it  was when combined with Comcast’s large cable operation as well as with the media assets of the company now known as Versant.

	Guthrie, however, enjoys tremendous standing at NBCUniversal. She is widely seen as a guiding force at “Today,” a signature program she co-anchors with Craig Melvin. While the morning-news audience is not what it once was decades ago, viewership is still seen as devoted and significant. The first two hours of “Today” — watched by around 3 million viewers each weekday — generated nearly $203.5 million in advertising in 2025, according to Guideline, a tracker of ad spending. Add the 9 a.m. and 10 a.m. hours to the mix, and NBC nabbed around $315.4 million from the weekday editions of the program.
	

	She also plays a key role in other parts of coverage, including the network’s recent Election Night that was the most-watched among the traditional TV-news outlets. What’s more, Guthrie is the host of a new  show based on the popular “Wordle” game from The New York Times slated to debut in coming months on NBC. “She’s fantastic,” says Jimmy Fallon, whose Electric Hot Dog production company is one of the backers of the program, during a recent interview with Variety.

	As of November 8, “Today” commanded 39% of the audience that has tuned in season to date for one of the three broadcast-network morning programs, according to data from Nielsen. It is well ahead of both ABC’s “Good Morning America” and CBS’ “CBS Mornings” in both overall viewership as well as among audiences between the ages of 25 and 54 — the demographic most coveted by advertisers in news programs.

	Guthrie can do hard-hitting newsmaker interviews and explain complicated legal matters, but also pal around with sports figures and movie stars. Internally, she is known for helping the “Today” personnel set the tone around each day’s news cycle. And she has helped NBC and “Today” during some of their greatest and most public trials.

	Guthrie’s presence as co-anchor helped the show move forward after the awkward exit of Ann Curry in 2012, which spurred a viewer backlash. When Matt Lauer was exiled in 2017 following revelations of “inappropriate sexual behavior,” Guthrie forged ahead, this time with Kotb in the seat beside her (Lauer has denied all allegations). Guthrie also helped NBC through a whirlwind in 2020 when the news division decided to hold a town hall with President Trump during his first term opposite an event ABC News arranged with then-candidate Joe Biden and George Stephanopoulos. Guthrie lifted the event out of publicity-stunt status by keeping the president to short answers — no small feat — and adding fact-checks and follow-ups. “‘You’re the president, you’re not like somebody’s crazy uncle who can retweet whatever,’” Guthrie told President Trump after asking why he recently retweeted a conspiracy theory.

	If Trump didn’t like the interview, he didn’t show it. He was among those offering to help the Guthrie family during their moment of crisis, bringing government help to bear in the search for Nancy Guthrie.
	

	The big TV-news outlets seem to be rethinking their stance on top anchors. To be sure, they have grown more interested in so-called “creators” — independent journalists, digital entrepreneurs and voice-y experts on specific topics — as younger consumers gravitate to video podcasts and e-mailed newsletters. But there is also more value in having a well-known and trusted persona available to give viewers the information they need. CBS News continues to work with Gayle King at its morning show, a recognition that her profile is hard-earned and not easily duplicated. The same is true of Norah O’Donnell, the former “CBS Evening News” anchor who has taken up new roles with both “CBS Mornings” and “60 Minutes.”

	It’s almost as if the networks have recognized that a strong relationship with viewers, once earned, is not to be spent lightly.

title: ‘Wolfenstein 3’ in Development at Xbox’s MachineGames
description:
“Wolfenstein 3″ is in the works at Xbox‘s Machine Games.

	Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced the news Thursday amid Xbox’s 25th anniversary celebratio
body:
“Wolfenstein 3″ is in the works at Xbox‘s Machine Games.

	Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced the news Thursday amid Xbox’s 25th anniversary celebration, sharing on X: “Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at @MachineGames. One of gaming’s most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more.”

	Sharma also shared a photo featuring a portion of a script for the project: 
	


	First launched in 1981 by Muse Software and later id Software, the “Wolfenstein” video game franchise is set in an alternate history World War II that largely follow U.S. Army captain William “B.J.” Blazkowicz in his fight against the Nazis. There are more than a dozen games in the series with the two most recent installments being reboots developed by MachineGames in partnership with publisher Bethesda Softworks: 2014’s “Wolfenstein: The New Order” and 2017’s “Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus.” 

	“Wolfenstein 3” will mark the first game in the franchise to be developed by MachineGames under Xbox ownership following Microsoft’s acquisition of parent company ZeniMax Media in March 2021.

	More to come…

title: ‘SVU’ Star Mariska Hargitay Breaks Down Benson and Stabler’s Complicated Reunion and Her Final Choice: ‘There Are So Many Feelings’
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers from the 600th episode of “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit.”

	To say that Olivia Benson and
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers from the 600th episode of “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit.”

	To say that Olivia Benson and Elliot Stabler have a complicated relationship would be an understatement. During the Nov. 12 600th episode of “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit,” Benson (Mariska Hargitay) is forced to reopen a case that she worked with Stabler (Christopher Meloni) many years ago, realizing they likely put the wrong man behind bars.
	

	After convincing him to come help her with the case, Benson learns that he had shut her out of the case and taken control, something she allowed him to do. But she’s the captain now — and isn’t going to allow their old patterns to return.

	“I love that we got to push up against each other because that’s also family. There are so many feelings between Benson and Stabler. It’s so complicated — what could have been, what was, what we’ve shared, the ‘ride or die,'” says Hargitay. “People ask, ‘Why do you think people love Benson and Stabler?’ And it’s because of their dedication to each other, their trust in each other.”

	Since Stabler “was so formative in her development as a detective,” this episode highlighted how they move past that. “It’s about a woman having her voice,” she says. “So many women identify with that.”

	Hargitay was excited to dive into such a strong storyline about the duo.

	“I think that we also just wanted to tell a truthful, complex story that people could identify with, have big feelings about, and understand the complexities of these types of relationships, and give them something real to go up against,” she adds. “We are so focused on keeping it real and making it good, and we know that just by being together, the fans will be happy. That’s why we invited him back because we knew they’d be so happy, and that’s what they would want. But also, he’s such a big part of the story. It’s truthful to have him back at this juncture.”
	

	At the end of the episode, Stabler invites Benson to take some time off and go away for a few days. The audience knows she has days off available, since it’s specifically mentioned early on, but that doesn’t mean she says yes. In fact, it was never even an option, says Hargitay.

	“No. There are a lot of reasons why not,” she says. “It’s not where they are now — either one of them.”

schema.headline: ‘SVU’ Star Mariska Hargitay Breaks Down Benson and Stabler’s Complicated Reunion and Her Final Choice: ‘There Are So Many Feelings’

title: Laika’s ‘Wildwood’ Passes $60 Million Worldwide (EXCLUSIVE)
description:

	After a sluggish start, the fantasy epic directed by Travis Knight has no
body:
Laika‘s stop-motion movie “Wildwood” has topped $60 million worldwide. 

	After a sluggish start, the fantasy epic directed by Travis Knight has now amassed a box office of $41.86 million in the U.S. and Canada and $19.06 million across 49 international territories.

	The milestone follows a strong third weekend in North America, where “Wildwood” grossed $7.21 million, declining 20% from the previous weekend despite a 13% reduction in its theatrical footprint, ranking as the number 2 holdover. Despite the solid hold, the total figure is still some way short of the film’s reported $100 million budget. 
	

	With almost $40 million earned in the U.S., “Wildwood” is Fathom Entertainment’s most successful release. The film has now exceeded the entire domestic theatrical run of DreamWorks/Universal’s “Forgotten Island” and tracks ahead of “The Boy and the Heron” and “Kubo and the Two Strings” at the same point in their theatrical releases. It will remain in 2,198 North American theatres for its fourth weekend. Desp

	“A PG-13 fantasy told in stop-motion is a rare thing to find in a theatre,” said David Burke, Laika’s chief marketing & operations officer and the film’s executive producer. “That’s part of the appeal of ‘Wildwood,’ and it’s also why a recommendation from someone who’s seen it carries so much weight. What’s encouraging about this third weekend is that audiences are now making the case for the film in their own words.”

	Added Jason Brenek, chief executive officer for Fathom Entertainmen: “‘Wildwood’ is maintaining its strong Fall box office performance and theatrical success, surpassing the Fathom feature film box office record previously held by Laika’s 15th anniversary re-release of Coraline in 2024.” Brenek added that there was “much more to come from this great film.”
	

	Inspired by Colin Meloy’s novel, “Wildwood” follows headstrong teenager Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee). After her baby brother is abducted by a murder of crows, she launches a desperate rescue mission into the Impassable Wilderness — an enchanted forest hidden just beyond Portland, Oregon. Joined by her hapless but loyal classmate Curtis Mehlberg (Jacob Tremblay), Prue navigates a world of talking animals, bandits, and powerful figures driven by grief and ambition. As the pair is drawn into a conflict threatening the balance of the forest itself, Prue must find a way to save her brother while confronting forces that could determine Wildwood’s future.

	International sales are handled by FilmNation Entertainment.

	“We’ve seen a resounding response from global audiences to Laika’s spectacular and unique world of Wildwood,” said founder and CEO of FilmNation Entertainment Glen Basner. “With more countries still to release, we know the enthusiasm for this extraordinary film, and the studio’s unmatched artistry, will continue to grow.”

title: ‘The Witcher’ Star Freya Allan to Lead Joachim Rønning’s Horror Movie ‘System’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “The Witcher” and “Planet of the Apes” star Freya Allan is set to star in “System,” the upcoming horror film from Norwegian director Joachim Rønnin
body:
“The Witcher” and “Planet of the Apes” star Freya Allan is set to star in “System,” the upcoming horror film from Norwegian director Joachim Rønning.

	Plot details remain under wraps, but production is currently underway on location in the old, abandoned underground stations and tunnels under London. Freya will be joined by Denzel Baidoo (“Last Swim”) and Felix Edwards (“MobLand”) in supporting roles.


	Rønning, who broke out with “Kon-Tiki” and would go on to direct major franchise titles including “Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales” and the recent “Tron: Ares,” will write, direct, and produce for The Saga Company. He penned the screenplay with his brother, Andreas Rønning.
	

	Roy Lee (“Weapons,” “It,” “The Ring”) and Steven Schneider (“Paranormal Activity,” “Insidious,” “Pet Sematary”) will produce for Spooky Pictures. Stewart le Maréchal and Anna Mohr-Pietsch produce for MetFilm. Image Nation Studios’ CEO Ben Ross (“Watcher,” “Company”), Spooky Pictures’ Rami Yasin (“Hokum”), and Andreas Rønning will executive produce.

	UTA Independent Film Group arranged the financing and is representing the film’s sale. 

	Under the Spooky Pictures-Image Nation Studios partnership, the companies have produced genre projects including “Late Night with the Devil,” Charlie Polinger’s “The Plague,” “Hokum” starring Adam Scott, Casey Affleck’s “Company” and Guy Nattiv’s “The Liberation.”

	Allan is perhaps best known for her role as Ciri, in Netflix’s global phenomenon “The Witcher,” a performance that earned her two Saturn Award nominations. She will return to her role for the fifth and final season, which is expected to release in late 2027. She recently finished shooting Nick Hamm’s |Black Palace” for Tempo Productions. Freya  also was seen leading Wes Ball’s “Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes,” the fourth instalment in the Planet of the Apes reboot series, with her acclaimed performance landing her a slot on Variety’s Power of Young Hollywood Impact Report in 2024.
	

	She is represented by CAA, United Agents, and Jackoway Austen Tyerman Wertheimer Mandelbaum Morris Bernstein Trattner Auerbach Hynick Jaime LeVine Sample & Klein. Rønning is represented by UTA and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern.

title: Chase Infiniti Coming-of-Age Drama ‘The Julia Set’ Sells Out for HanWay (EXCLUSIVE)
description: HanWay Films has sold out all territories globally for coming-of-age drama “The Julia Set,” starring “One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infi
body:
HanWay Films has sold out all territories globally for coming-of-age drama “The Julia Set,” starring “One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti, following its premiere in Toronto earlier this year. 

	As previously announced, Sony Pictures Classics acquired U.S. and key international territories including Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, the U.K., Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore) in a deal negotiated by HanWay Films and Gersh. 
	

	Additional sales now negotiated by HanWay Films include Sphere (Canada), Cinesky Pictures (Airlines), MegaCom Films (Former Yugoslavia), SND (France), Vuelta Germany (Germany), The Film Group (Greece), Synapse Distribution (Latin America), Front Row (Middle East), Kino Świat (Poland), Nos Lusomundo Audiovisuais (Portugal), Shaw Renters (Singapore) and Bir Film (Turkey).

	Directed by Niki Byrne, “The Julia Set” follows math prodigy Julia Fischer (Infiniti), who is recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics. At the same time, she begins to fall for her charismatic teaching assistant Pascal (Christopher Briney). As Pascal crumbles under the weight of his overbearing father Aleksander’s (Jason Isaacs) suffocating expectations, it is Pascal’s mother, Anne (Gillian Anderson), who helps Julia recognize and seize a moment of opportunity that will help to define her future.

	The film also stars Nina Hoss, Carmen Ejogo, Chloe Bailey, Nico Hiraga, Liz Lin and Alex Dillard.

	 “There are so many wonderful things I could say about HanWay, but nothing speaks louder than these three words: sold out, worldwide,” said Byrne. “Thank you to Gabrielle and her incredible team, and to our extraordinary partners in every territory, for believing in this film, and for giving Julia her passport.”
	

	Added Gabrielle Stewart, CEO of Hanway Films” “We are delighted to have such great partners for ‘The Julia Set’ globally. We look forward to working with SPC and all our partners on shaping a fantastic campaign for 2027. Congratulations to Niki Byrne and the whole team.”

	“The Julia Set” is produced by Potato Salad Cosmic Domination, Shaun Sanghani, in association with SSS Entertainment, G Nus Media, IF/THEN, Grapevine Films, Cinetrain SA, Melegrano Films, Hanway Films, Gotham Group, Good Future Films and Vacancy Film Fund. Producers include Jeffrey Penman, Nick Scherma, Shaun Sanghani, Anderson, Eleonora Granata Jenkinson, Andrey Epifanov, David Treatman, Max Johnson, Lee Stollman, Ellen Goldsmith-Vein and Tayler Haynes.\

	“From Niki’s first draft to TIFF to today, The Julia Set has kept finding the right people,” said Scherma and Penman. “We’re endlessly grateful to Gabrielle and the HanWay team, to SPC, and to every partner who has taken Julia on. We can’t wait for audiences everywhere to meet her in 2027.”

	Executive producers include Margaret Black, Nicole G. Small, Infiniti, Cecily Colahan, Gabriel Jenkinson, Kenneth Yu, Vico Sharabani, Natalia Gurova, David Koenig, Joey Suquet, Phil Hunt, Harsimranjit “Harry” Ahluwalla, Ryan Lewis, Stephen Lamm, Michael Cassutt, Jonah Minkove, Debra Taweel, J. Todd Harris, Art Williams, Chad Oliver, Daniel Sheldon, David Fensterstock and Russell Posternak. Co-producers are DJ Dodd, Paolo Pilladi, Rob Simmons and Mitchell Darwin.

title: Documentaries at the Oscars: A History of Breaking Out of Their Category — and What It Means for ‘You Can See Everything’
description:
A documentary is a film, too. But at the Oscars, it still hasn’t been fully embraced as one.

	One of the breakout hits of the awards season is A24
body:
A documentary is a film, too. But at the Oscars, it still hasn’t been fully embraced as one.

	One of the breakout hits of the awards season is A24’s insanely entertaining “You Can See Everything” from directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, which had a surprise world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival in September and opened in theaters Oct. 16, grossing nearly $80 million at the domestic box office through its fourth weekend. Many professional pundits and awards enthusiasts are predicting the film will make history as the first documentary feature to land a best picture nomination. So we looked at the history of nonfiction films at the Academy Awards to see which movies have been embraced by the various branches and categories (some now defunct) over the years and what that history says about the film’s chances.
	

	Across 98 ceremonies, feature docs have earned a total of 33 nominations in categories other than documentary feature, according to the Academy’s own statistics. Three of them won statuettes.Of the 14 nominations nonfiction films have collected outside their own race since 2013 (the 85th ceremony), 10 have come in best original song. 

	The documentary feature category is decided by members of the Documentary Branch, which was formed in 2001 and, according to the Academy’s most recent figures, has 719 voting members, making it the third-largest branch behind Actors (1,202) and Executives (759). Preliminary voting runs Dec. 7-11, narrowing the field to a 15-film shortlist that will be announced Dec. 15. Members of the branch will then vote from that list in January to determine the five nominees, which will be revealed Jan. 21.
	

	The Academy has 19 branches, and each nominates within its own discipline. At the same time, the entire voting membership chooses best picture nominees. Although Academy rules do not expressly prohibit documentaries from competing in other categories, nonfiction films rarely factor into races that presume fictional storytelling, including production design, costume design and acting. This year, A24 is pushing “You Can See Everything” in 11 categories, including best picture, director, supporting actress and documentary feature. Its awards site initially listed the film in the artisan races of production design (Alex DiGerlando and Rebecca Meis), cinematography (David Bolen), costume design (Katina Danabassis), film editing (Adam Locke-Norton), makeup and hairstyling (Stephanie Pasicov and Kerrie Smith), sound (Paul Hsu and Richard Carlos) and original score (Ari Balouzian). However, an updated version of the site no longer lists production design, costume design, makeup and hairstyling or sound. As Variety previously reported, Seyfried’s acting turn is eligible for the Oscars and Critics Choice but not for BAFTA, SAG (The Actor Awards) and the Golden Globes Awards.

	No documentary has ever been nominated for best picture or best director. The closest came at the inaugural Oscars, when “Chang: A Drama of the Wilderness” (1927), the jungle drama shot on location in Siam by Merian C. Cooper and Ernest B. Schoedsack (the duo who would later make 1933’s “King Kong”), was nominated for unique and artistic picture, one of two top prizes handed out that night.

	Two years later, “With Byrd at the South Pole” (1930), an account of Richard E. Byrd’s 1928-30 Antarctic expedition, won cinematography for Joseph T. Rucker and Willard Van Der Veer, becoming the first documentary to win an Oscar more than a decade before the Academy created a category for the form. A documentary category was introduced at the 1942 ceremony, with features and shorts competing together. The two were split into separate categories in 1944.

	The writers branch took notice in the late 1940s, nominating Robert and Frances Flaherty’s story for “Louisiana Story” (1948), about a young Cajun boy and his pet raccoon and the story and screenplay of Sidney Meyers’ “The Quiet One” (1949), which blends real-life locations with staged scenes to tell the story of Donald Peters, a 10-year-old Black boy from Harlem grappling with severe emotional trauma. They remain the only two documentaries ever nominated for writing, with “The Quiet One” competing in the category then known as writing (story and screenplay).
	

	Norman Foster’s “Navajo” (1952), about a young Navajo boy caught in a clash of cultures, made history as the first film nominated for both documentary feature and cinematography, with Virgil E. Miller cited in the black-and-white category.

	The music branch embraced nonfiction scores early on and continued to do so for more than three decades.

	Louis Gruenberg’s music for “The Fight for Life” (1940) opened the door, followed by Disney’s wartime hybrid “Victory Through Air Power” (1943) by Edward H. Plumb, Paul J. Smith and Oliver G. Wallace; the Cinerama showcase “This Is Cinerama” (1953) by Louis Forbes; Disney’s True-Life Adventures entries “Perri” (1957) by Paul Smith and “White Wilderness” (1958) by Oliver Wallace; the U.K. import “The Bolshoi Ballet” (1958) by Yuri Faier and G. Rozhdestvensky; and, finally, Gerald Fried’s work on “Birds Do It, Bees Do It” (1975), the last time a documentary score was recognized, more than 50 years ago.

	The lone winner of score in that era was “Let It Be” (1970), which took home the original song score for the Beatles, giving the band its first and only Oscar.

	Michael Wadleigh’s three-hour music chronicle “Woodstock” (1970) remains the gold standard for crossover recognition. Wadleigh’s concert landmark won documentary feature and earned nominations for film editing (Thelma Schoonmaker, years before her three wins for Martin Scorsese) and sound (Dan Wallin and Larry Johnson). Its three total nominations are still tied with “Flee” for the most ever received by a documentary.

	The second editing nomination came 24 years later, when Steve James’ “Hoop Dreams” (1994) was famously shut out of the documentary feature category at the 67th Oscars, even as the editors branch nominated Frederick Marx, James and Bill Haugse. The snub became one of the most notorious in Academy history and helped force a rethink of how the documentary branch selected its nominees.The craft branches have largely closed their doors to nonfiction films since. No documentary has been nominated in cinematography since 1953, in sound since 1971 or in film editing since 1995.

	If there is a side door for nonfiction today, it’s the original song category. Twelve documentaries have received nominations for best original song: “Mondo Cane” (1963), for Riz Ortolani and Nino Oliviero’s “More”; “An Inconvenient Truth” (2006), for Melissa Etheridge’s “I Need to Wake Up,” the only song from a documentary to win; “Chasing Ice” (2012), for J. Ralph’s “Before My Time”; “Glen Campbell … I’ll Be Me” (2014), for Glen Campbell and Julian Raymond’s “I’m Not Gonna Miss You”; “The Hunting Ground” (2015), for Diane Warren and Lady Gaga’s “Til It Happens to You”; “Racing Extinction” (2015), for Ralph and Anohni’s “Manta Ray”; “Jim: The James Foley Story” (2016), for Ralph and Sting’s “The Empty Chair”; “RBG” (2018), for Warren’s “I’ll Fight”; “American Symphony” (2023), for Jon Batiste and Dan Wilson’s “It Never Went Away”; “Elton John: Never Too Late” (2024), for Elton John, Brandi Carlile, Andrew Watt and Bernie Taupin’s “Never Too Late”; “Diane Warren: Relentless” (2025), for Warren’s “Dear Me”; and “Viva Verdi!” (2025), for Nicholas Pike’s “Sweet Dreams of Joy.”
	

	Etheridge’s win came more than four decades after “Mondo Cane” opened the door, and “An Inconvenient Truth” also took documentary feature that night. Davis Guggenheim’s climate film remains the only documentary feature winner to also win an Oscar in another category, and it is the last documentary of any kind to win outside its own race.

	The more telling number is this one: 10 of the 12 documentary song nominees came from films the documentary branch passed over. Only “An Inconvenient Truth” and “RBG” were nominated in both categories. For distributors of music-driven or celebrity-centered docs, the math is plain. The song campaign is often the more realistic path to the Dolby Theatre than the documentary race itself, as “American Symphony,” “Elton John: Never Too Late” and “Viva Verdi!” (a portrait of Milan’s Casa Verdi retirement home, with its nominated aria sung by Puerto Rican soprano Ana María Martínez) all demonstrated.

	The other modern avenue runs through international feature, where a film needs its country’s official submission before Academy voters can weigh in.

	Ari Folman’s animated documentary “Waltz With Bashir” (2008) broke through first, nominated for foreign language film for Israel at the 81st Oscars, though it missed documentary feature. A decade later, three straight years of history followed. North Macedonia’s “Honeyland” (2019) became the first film nominated for both documentary feature and international feature at the 92nd ceremony. Alexander Nanau’s “Collective” (2020) repeated the feat the following year and gave Romania its first Oscar nomination ever. Then Jonas Poher Rasmussen’s Danish feature “Flee” (2021) became the first film nominated in documentary feature, animated feature and international feature in the same year.

	None of the three won anything.

	“Honeyland” lost to “American Factory” (2019) and “Parasite” (2019), “Collective” fell to “My Octopus Teacher” (2020) and “Another Round” (2020), and “Flee” went 0-for-3 against “Summer of Soul” (2021), “Encanto” (2021) and “Drive My Car” (2021). Four ceremonies have passed since “Flee” without another documentary in the international lineup.

	So what does nearly a century of history tell us about “You Can See Everything?”
	

	For starters, the doors that have opened for nonfiction have mostly been in craft and music races and those are precisely the categories where A24 has trimmed and focused its campaign. The film has already swept the Critics Choice Documentary Awards, winning all five categories in which it was nominated. But the Academy has been a tougher nut to crack. 

	Best picture is a different animal. The documentary branch doesn’t decide it. The full voting membership, now more than 10,000 industry professionals, does. That cuts both ways. A film the documentary branch might view with suspicion, as it once did “Hoop Dreams,” can still find support among actors, executives and craftspeople who simply loved the movie. The music branch has already shown that pattern 10 times over, nominating songs from documentaries the doc branch passed over. It isn’t far-fetched to imagine “You Can See Everything” landing in best picture while missing documentary feature altogether, a scenario already being floated this season.

	Variety’s latest Oscar predictions have “You Can See Everything” earning three nominations: best picture, supporting actress for Seyfried and film editing. Notably absent is documentary feature, a category in which many pundits believe its omission would rank among the branch’s most significant snubs, alongside such overlooked films as “Won’t You Be My Neighbor” (2018), “Jane” (2017), “Stories We Tell” (2012), etc. But even a fraction of that predicted crossover haul would rewrite the Oscar record books.

	The first major test comes Dec. 15, when the documentary shortlist is announced, followed by Oscar nominations on Jan. 21. If “You Can See Everything” breaks through in even one of the Academy’s other races, it would mark a significant milestone for A24.

	Because, hey, a documentary is a film, too.

schema.headline: Documentaries at the Oscars: A History of Breaking Out of Their Category — and What It Means for ‘You Can See Everything’

title: ‘Oh, Mary!’ Mania Takes Over L.A.: Director Sam Pinkleton on Bringing the Unruly Broadway Comedy Phenomenon to Full Houses at the Ahmanson
description: As most theater fans already know, “Oh, Mary!,” which is as hysterical as it is ahistorical, is the story of possibly unhinged presidential spouse
body:
As most theater fans already know, “Oh, Mary!,” which is as hysterical as it is ahistorical, is the story of possibly unhinged presidential spouse Mary Todd Lincoln, and her thwarted aspirations to escape life in the parlors of the White House for a career in show business. If there is anything Mary would appreciate, it’s a bigger room. So she would be deeply pleased with the production of “Oh, Mary!” that opens this week at L.A.’s Ahmanson Theatre, where the vast majority of seats for its nearly month-long run sold out in advance. That’s not something that happens with every engagement in the 2,100-seat theater, but Mary — and “Mary” — are a unique case, to say the least.
	

	The wild comedic play, directed by Sam Pinkleton and written by (and originally starring) Cole Escola, became Broadway’s toughest ticket immediately upon opening in early 2024, after a smash off-Broadway run. The succession of actors eager to step into Mary’s dress in the last two and a half years has included both drag performers and cis women. On the national tour that is arriving in L.A., the leading lady is the indelicately named drag queen Alaska Thunderfuck, who has some big 19th century shoes to slip into. Even bigger, maybe, since she has a vaster balcony to project to than the one in Broadway’s Lyceum, which has less than half the L.A. theater’s capacity. But in an interview with Variety, Pinkleton suggests that putting “Oh, Mary!” in a larger space might work to the show’s advantage, given the potential contagion of that many ticketholders getting caught up in uncontrolled laughter, as tends to happen as the show grows progressively more outrageous.
	

	Pinkleton is already known to some L.A. audiences for his 2024 Pasadena Playhouse production of “La Cage aux Folles,” and Broadway theatergoers are currently catching his revival of “The Rocky Horror Show” as well as “Oh, Mary!” He also talked with Variety about two other classic musicals he is set to bring back to New York. But first, his thoughts on bringing the thunder to L.A.’s Music Center. (Incidentally, the Ahmanson just announced that the demand for “Oh, Mary!” tickets will result in the show making a return engagement in 2027, for those with FOMO about missing out on the good seats this time.)

	Sometimes, when we do a piece about a play coming in, we say something about how we’ll be “helping spread the news.” It might sound silly to say that about this show, though — ust about everyone in L.A. knows that it’s coming.

	Well, that’s because there are so many flags on flag poles. It’s like a fascist “Oh, Mary!” state with all of those “Oh, Mary!” flags everywhere.

	The tour has been in San Francisco, Portland and Seattle on its way to the Ahmanson. Assuming you must have come out west to see how it’s doing at at least one of those stops, any thoughts on how it’s working as a touring show?

	I love this version of the show, and I’m not just saying that because it’s my job to say it to you right now. It’s because we’ve seen the play with so many different people, we’ve kind of learned how it can stretch, and I think that this version of the play is the play. I feel very happy with it. It feels like the play that Cole wrote. It feels like the play that I directed. They’re an incredible company; Alaska is so funny. I was a bit nervous about it in these big theaters, but I saw it in San Francisco at the Curran, and the play is not what one would call subtle, so it really works in these big rooms. It’s also just so fun to be with that many people laughing. So I’m sure that it will curse us because I said this to you, but I feel like it’s going pretty well.

	So many of us are curious about how it will feel because you’ve got such a perfect jewel box environment there in New York. But you feel like, from what you’ve been able to see, you get a similar reaction?

	Yeah. And you know, the big jump for us was from off-Broadway to Broadway. That was like: What the hell? How is this gonna work in a big theater? Because the Lyceum, the Broadway theater, is small, but it’s very tall, and I honestly thought it was gonna be a disaster on Broadway. I really thought it wouldn’t translate. But I actually think it plays better on Broadway than it did in a small theater. So running it on Broadway has given us the confidence to know how to kind of fill a room with it, and the adaptations we’ve made for the tour, I think, account for the different spaces very smartly.
	

	I also think sometimes it’s easy to kind of insult the audiences at these big theaters. But if you go to the theater in Charlotte, a 3,000-seat theater, that’s your theater. That’s how you experience theater, so the fact that it is at that scale isn’t weird. You know, that’s how I met theater. I grew up in Richmond, Virginia, going to national tours, and I’m sure I saw tiny shows that got swallowed up by that big stage, but it was where I saw theater. So I feel very positive about it being in all of these massive theaters.



	

					‘Oh, Mary!’ at the Ahmanson Theatre in Los Angeles
									Evan Zimmerman
	



	Occasionally I go onto Broadway message boards…

	Wow, brave man.

	…and before I ever got to see the show in New York, I was looking up message threads about “Oh, Mary!” to see whether the reaction was uniformly positive. It was, almost, but there was one discussion that had a header along the lines of, “Am I the only person who didn’t get ‘Oh, Mary!’?” He was confused that everyone in the entire theater was rolling in the aisles except for him. And it made for interesting reading, because a lot of the respondents were basically saying, “Yes, it’s just you… but I really expected there to be a lot more of you. I saw this off-Broadway and loved it but thought it would just appeal to downtowners or the gay comunity.” So people were saying they loved it but they were shocked that everyone else loves it. Obviously you knew that it had a broad appeal, but were you even a little bit surprised at how broad?

	I definitely didn’t know it had a broad appeal at all. I think I was on the far side of cynicism there. We made it for a short run downtown, and were delighted that our dumb friends wanted to come, and that was enough, you know? It was like, mission accomplished! We got some gay people to laugh. Hooray! And it wasn’t until we were on Broadway, early on, that I looked around at a matinee and was like, “These people are not gay people from Brooklyn. These people are, like, Aunt Kathy who took the train in and wanted to see a Broadway show.” And Aunt Kathy deserves to have a good time, and God bless her. Aunt Kathy’s laughing at dick jokes, and that felt great. I watched my conservative father watch the show, and he was howling.

	I think there could be a lot of explanations for that, but I think at its root, there’s something really old-fashioned about “Oh, Mary!” When people come to me and are like, “It’s groundbreaking, it’s radical!,” I’m like, “It’s actually not. It’s a play with a couch.” I think it’s well-written and I’m very proud of it, but fundamentally it’s a play with a couch, and you’ve seen a play with a couch before. So like I think the elements of it are familiar in a way that make it kind of approachable. It has a bit of Carol Burnett in it, it has a bit of “The Muppet Show” in it, it has a bit of “I Love Lucy” in it. So I didn’t expect it to have the appeal that it has, but I love that it does, and I love, love, love seeing audiences that you wouldn’t expect at this play laugh at some of these jokes. In Hartford, Connecticut, I was like, “How is this gonna go,” watching these older ladies, and they were so into it.
	

	The pure physicality in a few scenes, where the audience in New York was just having waves of laughter, reminded me of seeing some of the old Sid Caesar “Your Show of Shows” sketches from early TV days where the live audience is practically going insane. But that’s part of the rollercoaster ride that the audience goes on, where the audience knows it’s going be outrageous, but it still surprises them with how outrageous.

	Yeah. We try to really protect the secrets of it. And part of the fun of it is getting hit with those surprises.

	Let’s talk casting. Why is Alaska Thunderfuck so great for this?

	Well, Alaska’s known to most as a beloved, famous drag queen, and that she is. But I know Alaska as a great actress. We’ve done a few musicals together, and from the early days when Cole and I started to realize that other people were gonna play this part, Alaska was one of the first names that I brought up. She really can do it all. The thing that is so amazing to me about her is she has this super over-the-top, wacky, absurd public persona. But she is the most disciplined, rigorous performer. There’s no detail too small for her. She works so hard and is such a pro. And she has approached this like a drama — like she’s just a great actress in a drama. It makes it so funny, because she’s 1,000 feet tall and she’s in this massive dress, throwing herself all around, but she’s taking it so seriously.



	

					‘Oh, Mary!’ at the Ahmanson Theatre in Los Angeles
									Evan Zimmerman
	



	A lot of people who are fans of the show probably wish that they could see every production of this with every actor, because it’s easy to imagine how wildly different all these Marys would be. It was originated as a role played in drag but you also have cis women doing it. When did you start thinking about how much you could open this up to different types of actors or actresses?

	It was sort of a puzzle that was born out of necessity. We really didn’t think much about other people doing it, other than the amazing Hannah Solow, who was originally the standby and went on to take over the part for a while on Broadway. But when we knew that we were gonna keep running on Broadway and Cole needed to take a break, we were like, “Somebody else has to do it.” And Cole and I always took the play very seriously as a dramatic work, even if nobody else did, and so we wanted to make sure the first replacement for Cole wasn’t just a wacky person in a dress. And Betty Gilpin came up, who I think is one of our greatest living actors, and Betty completely got it and approached it like she was doing Chekhov, and it was so, so funny. By having Betty be the first replacement, I think it taught us how good the play is. Then the fun of it has been kind of bouncing… like, making your next move as far from the thing that came before it as possible. So we’ve been able to go from Betty to Jinkx Monsoon to Titus Burgess to Jane Krakowski to… You know, it’s just that Cole wrote a good play, so it can hold a lot.
	

	Just in terms of the sort of extreme turns of the play, which we won’t reveal, I found myself in that tension of wondering if we should identify with Mary, or do we worry that she should be institutionalized immediately for psychosis? Or do we identify with her because she’s kind of psychotic and we have a psychotic side? We go along with her as she acts out in these repressive or strict situations, and it’s not always clear whether to cheer her on or recoil, though it’s understood we’re going to be on her side.

	Yeah, I think many of the people who have played Mary… I’m gonna use as an example the great Meg Stalter, who did it on Broadway. The first thing Meg said to me was, “I’ve never seen myself on stage before like that.” And I do think that a lot of the Marys in particular really relate to her, and I think we all can relate to a feeling of being trapped somewhere — a feeling of believing something about yourself so intensely that everybody else thinks is a joke. I mean, I’m not trying to be funny. I do think it’s quite relatable. And there are some things in the play where she gets really honest, and I think on the best of days, those are played with complete truth. So I do think she’s an unlikely hero, but I root for her. Obviously it’s great when people laugh at the play, but I love when people are moved by it. And it can be surprising.

	It’s good you mention that, because there is one scene in the play where a lot of us find ourselves thinking, “Wow, this got really kind of earnest for a minute.”

	It’s super earnest.

	It’s always interesting when things that tend toward outrageousness or even slapstick get briefly sort of serious before the comedy kicks in again. I always think of the movie “Kingpin,” where there is one scene in the middle where the main character talks about his unhappy childhood or something, and there is no laugh in the scene at all — like, “for whatever reason, we’re gonna ground you for just a minute before we go back to being bonkers.” And “Oh, Mary!” reminded me of that. Maybe Mary is an anti-heroine for all of us.

	Yeah. I mean, she does outrageous things, but her situation… Maybe being the wife of Abraham Lincoln is not relatable, but I think a lot about her situation is relatable, very broadly.
	

	You said somewhere recently that “The Rocky Horror Show” was your 10th Broadway show. Is that right? That’s a lot.

	Somehow that is true. It is my 10th Broadway show.

	You’ve had breakthroughs and popular hits before, but as an actual phenomenon, does “Oh, Mary!” feel like the biggest thing in your career at this point?

	You know, I’ve had a lot of shows do well. I’ve also had a lot of shows not do well. But what has happened with “Oh, Mary!” and the way that it has kind of caught fire culturally is unique. I’m not a spring chicken, but I’m not on the rocking chair on the porch yet, you know? I’ve got a lot of energy left. And I’ve said to so many people involved in “Oh, Mary!” who have this ss their first Broadway show or their first play, “Guys, it isn’t usually like this. Don’t get used to this.”

	So I can see how “Oh, Mary!” is unique in the success of it, but also, the thing I like about my job is directing, and directing is kind of the same whether you’re doing it in a basement in a church in Iowa or on a Broadway stage. So there’s a way that “Oh, Mary!” stands out, and there’s also a way that I just like making shows, you know? I like making shows, and I make a lot of shows, and I’m making a lot of shows right now, and I’m very grateful that “Oh, Mary!” gets to continue to be one of the shows that I’m making.



	

					Sam Pinkleton attends “Oh, Mary” Opening Night at Lyceum Theatre on July 11, 2024 in New York City. (Photo by Michael Loccisano/Getty Images)
									Getty Images
	



	You’ve had a lot going on, including “The Rocky Horror Show” on Broadway right now, but is there more in the pipeline for you?

	I’m doing a lot. I’m opening a musical in London that I love so much it hurts, which is called “Ceilidh,” which is an unspellable word. It’s a Scottish participatory dance musical. I’m doing “You’re a Good Man, Charlie Brown” at City Center with David Hyde Pierce, Ayo Edebiri and Danielle Brooks, this crazy cast. And then next year I’m going to direct the 50th anniversary Broadway revival of “Annie,” which is kind of a demented cousin of “Oh, Mary!”

	A cousin how?

	Oh, my goodness. I mean, you used the word “earnest” to describe a moment in “Oh, Mary!,” which I really love, and I think that there is an incredible sincerity to “Oh, Mary!” and an incredible exuberance to “Oh, Mary!” I really don’t have a lot of curiosity in things that roll their eyes. I just think the world is cynical enough without us making cynical things inside of it. And so “Annie,” much like “Oh, Mary!,” is just bright-eyed and exuberant and nasty, and it behaves badly, and it’s got teeth. I’m really excited about it. People always think I’m kidding when I say I’m excited about it. I’m like, “No, no, no, I’m so excited about it.” “Annie” is badass.
	

	And what excites you about “Charlie Brown”?

	Oh, gosh. I mean, I find the world of Charles Schulz to be so devastating and honest. And “You’re a Good Man, Charlie Brown” is as if Samuel Beckett wrote a musical. It’s so quietly devastatingly existential and sweet, and not cloying. When I started thinking about doing it with adults, and in particular with David Hyde Pierce as Charlie Brown, I was really moved by the simplicity of it. That’s the whole thing with Charles Schulz: Hpw can you kind of say the most with the least? That is, I think, kind of an amazing challenge to make theater with, and it’s not how I usually make theater. I’m usually kind of a maximalist. And “You’re a Good Man, Charlie Brown,” by virtue of Charles Schulz, is this invitation to be incredibly emotionally rich and also very spare with how we tell the story. I’m really excited about it. It’s so sweet.

schema.headline: ‘Oh, Mary!’ Mania Takes Over L.A.: Director Sam Pinkleton on Bringing the Unruly Broadway Comedy Phenomenon to Full Houses at the Ahmanson

            Anthony Clark, the comedian and actor best known for starring on "Yes, Dear," reportedly died from complications related to pneumonia.
      
    
            The 62-year-old actor died Tuesday, with Deadline now reporting pneumonia complications were behind his death.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... Clark's former "Yes, Dear" costar Mike O'Malley announced his death Wednesday on X, remembering him as a "hilarious guy" and a standout comedian in Boston's comedy scene.
      

            O'Malley revealed the two had spoken on the phone just three weeks before Clark's death ... saying his longtime friend had him laughing once again.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Clark was best known for playing Greg Warner opposite O'Malley's Jimmy Hughes on the CBS sitcom, which ran for six seasons from 2000 to 2006.
      
    
            He also starred in "Boston Common," appeared in films including "The Rock" and hosted the fourth season of "Last Comic Standing."

title: NBA Star Chris Bosh Linked to Palisades Fire Case by Arson Suspect's Defense
description:
Palisades Fire
                          What's Chris Bosh Got to Do with It?!
body:
Palisades Fire
                          What's Chris Bosh Got to Do with It?!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 12, 2026
                            6:06 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Jonathan Rinderknecht lawyer is trying to prove he didn't start 2025's deadly Palisades fire ... and is pointing a finger at Chris Bosh's mansion instead.
      
    
            According to court documents obtained by the California Post, Rinderknecht's lawyer wants to introduce testimony from retired Cal Fire investigator Michael T. Cole about a possible firework launched from the NBA star's house.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The filing said ... "Mr. Cole is expected to testify that during his 2025 investigation of the Palisades Fire he observed and documented a mark and an associated burn and smoke trail on the driveway and rear patio area of the residence at (redacted), and that, based on his training and experience, those marks are physical evidence of a launched firework."
      

            The former Miami Heat star was reportedly renting out the house when the fires started, according to The Post.
      
    
            Prosecutors slammed the request in their own filing, saying Cole has "zero qualifications, training, or experience."
      
    
            They said ... "His entire 'expert' opinion is based on six drone photographs of a brown stain on the driveway taken in either February 2025 or 2026. No up-close in-person inspection, no other testing. Six drone photographs, that’s it."
      
    
            Rinderknecht's defense for the re-trial argues that fireworks possibly caused the devastating blaze ... not him.
      
    
            As you know, Rinderknecht is accused of sparking the blaze by using his lighter to set vegetation on fire. He's denying the allegations.

description:

                          Killed By Gang Members ...

body:
12-Year-Old Boy
                          Killed By Gang Members ...
                          While They Targeted Rival Gang Member
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 12, 2026
                            4:30 PM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 12, 2026
                                5:24 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Three alleged gang members are facing federal charges after prosecutors say they shot at a car they believed belonged to a rival gang member ... but instead ended up killing an innocent 12-year-old boy named Kade Lewin.
      
    
            24-year-old Ousmane Diallo, 26-year-old Mayel Bussereth and 25-year-old Jonah Luc are charged with racketeering and firearm-related offenses in connection with the deadly 2022 Brooklyn shooting.
      
    
            Prosecutors claim that on March 31, 2022, the three men who are alleged members of the ICG Barbiez gang drove around looking for a rival gang member.
      

            Per court docs, the three men allegedly drove around the block near East 56th Street and Linden Boulevard several times, apparently searching for their target ... before finally spotting a parked car they believed a rival was sitting inside.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Prosecutors allege they opened fire on the car ... but their intended target wasn't inside. The alleged gang members shot 12-year-old Kade, who was sitting in the vehicle when the bullets came flying. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
      
    
            Another innocent bystander was also caught in the gunfire, but survived.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            If convicted, the three gang members could face the death penalty.

Orville Peck
                          Duets With Ex-NFL Star Carl Nassib
                          Amid Raider Kiss Speculation
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Orville Peck brought former NFL player Carl Nassib out with him for duet of "Something to Talk About" ... and let's just say they really gave us something to talk about!
      
    
            The two sang Bonnie Raitt's hit at Philly's Metropolitan Opera House Wednesday ... wearing matching black tanks tucked into black jeans.
      
    
      
      Carl Nassib gay perfeito https://t.co/KcvrvXiJI7
              @tjoshua_tree
          
  
    
            Their eyebrow-raising duet comes after Orville admitted he made out with a Las Vegas Raiders player in his recent song "Ring the Bell."
      

                    
                          
                                  
      
        
    
            Orville croons in the song ... "I love the Lakers, the Mets and the Longhorns, made out with a guy on the Raiders."
      
    
            Carl is not only a former player for the Raiders ... he's also the first NFL star to come out as gay.
      
    
            Orville previously told Variety that he got permission to sing about the mystery Raider back in September ... but he declined to reveal his identity to the publication.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            He added ... "This person would have probably allowed me to say their name if I wanted, but I didn’t think it was necessary. People can use their own common sense and discovery to try to figure out who it may be, but that’s all I’ll say."
      
    
            This duet may very well be the common-sense confirmation fans had hoped for.
